title: N.Y. or L.A.

jokes.text: Hank reads the applause sign as 'applesauce' to warm up the audience, then immediately corrects himself: 'No. No. No, I'm kidding. It says applause.'
jokes.setup: Hank is warming up the studio audience, pointing to the sign that says 'APPLAUSE'
jokes.punchline: He announces it says 'applesauce,' then walks back the absurdity with a flat 'I'm kidding'
jokes.explanation: A mild, functional warm-up gag that fits Hank's slightly desperate, crowd-pleasing persona. The flat correction 'No. No. No, I'm kidding.' is funnier than the joke itself — classic Hank. Not original but competently executed.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That sign says, 'applesauce.' No. No. No, I'm kidding. It says, 'applause.'

jokes.text: Hank's announcer intro for Larry: 'and now, because he desperately needs your approval... Larry Sanders!'
jokes.setup: Standard late-night announcer intro building anticipation for the host
jokes.punchline: Instead of a flattering superlative, Hank punctures Larry with brutal psychological accuracy: 'because he desperately needs your approval'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. It perfectly encapsulates the entire show's thesis — Larry's narcissism and need for validation — delivered as a throwaway announcer line. The specificity ('desperately needs your approval') makes it cut. On rewatch, knowing Larry's arc, it lands even harder. High character integration: this line only works for Larry Sanders.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: and now, because he desperately needs your approval, Larry Sanders!

jokes.text: Larry addresses the rumor the network is for sale: 'The buyer came in during the evening and found only $20 in the register and passed.'
jokes.setup: Larry is doing desk monologue material about rumors the network is for sale, playing it as newsworthy
jokes.punchline: The punchline reframes the network as so valueless a buyer was scared off by $20 in the register — like a failing convenience store
jokes.explanation: Sharp monologue joke that works on two levels: it's funny as industry satire and it's funny as a glimpse into Larry's real anxiety about his network's instability. The '$20 in the register' image is specific and economical. Solid professional-grade monologue writing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The buyer came in During the evening And, uh, found only $20 in the register And passed.

jokes.text: Larry dismisses the CBS Evening News story because 'Connie' filed it, then says 'Her husband Maury has more credibility as far as I'm concerned.'
jokes.setup: A staffer tells Larry the network sale story broke on the CBS Evening News. Larry asks 'who did the story, Connie or Dan?'
jokes.punchline: Larry dismisses Connie Chung's credibility by invoking Maury Povich — her tabloid TV husband — as the more credible journalist
jokes.explanation: Good insider showbiz joke. The inversion — dismissing a network anchor by praising her tabloid-TV husband — is clever and specific to the era (early '90s). Loses a little on 'earned_vs_cheap' because it leans on name recognition. Solid monologue beat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Her husband maury Has more credibility As far as I'm concerned.

jokes.text: Hank's non-sequitur: 'Welcome to the monkey house. Pass the penis, please. Am I right?'
jokes.setup: Larry has wrapped up the monologue segment on the network-sale topic with 'Business as usual, same old shit.'
jokes.punchline: Hank attempts to button the bit with an incoherent, enthusiastic non-sequitur that means absolutely nothing
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout lines. Hank's word-salad enthusiasm — 'Welcome to the monkey house. Pass the penis, please. Am I right?' — is perfectly calibrated absurdism. It's funny because it's meaningless AND because it's delivered with complete conviction. The fact that Larry's immediate response is to offer 'transcripts so we can all try to figure out what Hank meant at our leisure' makes it a two-part joke with a beautifully deadpan button. High quotability, high character integration — only Hank Kingsley says something this confidently idiotic.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Welcome to the monkey house. Pass the penis, please. Am I right?

jokes.text: Larry: 'Later I'll pass out some transcripts so we can all try to figure out what Hank meant at our leisure.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just said 'Welcome to the monkey house. Pass the penis, please. Am I right?' on air
jokes.punchline: Larry doesn't panic or scold — he deadpans an offer to distribute transcripts for post-show analysis, as if this is a normal protocol
jokes.explanation: Larry's comeback is almost as good as the original Hank absurdism. The phrase 'at our leisure' is doing serious comedic work — it implies this is a recurring problem that requires a structured institutional response. Perfect economy, perfect character voice. The joke requires Hank's preceding non-sequitur to land, making it a true callback/reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Later i'll pass out Some transcripts So we can all Try to figure out What Hank meant At our leisure.

jokes.text: Artie to Larry backstage: 'People can't do their best work when they're shitting in their pants.'
jokes.setup: Larry admits he hated lying to his staff about the network situation. Artie is justifying the decision.
jokes.punchline: Artie's blunt, vulgar rationale for keeping staff in the dark — delivered with total authority
jokes.explanation: Classic Artie — pragmatic, crude, delivered with the gravity of a life lesson. It's funny because it's simultaneously good management advice AND deeply inelegant. The vulgarity is earned by his character. Rip Torn's delivery would sell this perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: When people lie, They tend to cover their mouths. I learned that From jack webb when I was on dragnet, 1970.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Yeah, well, maybe that's why I haven't been able to focus this week.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just said people can't work while 'shitting in their pants'
jokes.punchline: Larry applies the metaphor to himself with unintentional self-deprecation, implying he too has been metaphorically incontinent with anxiety
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat — Larry inadvertently admitting he's as paralyzed as the staff he's trying to protect. A small, quiet laugh. The self-awareness without fully registering it is very Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: What are you listed under, Hank or Kingsley? Or hey, now?

jokes.text: Artie warns Larry about lying tells: 'Rubbing your upper lip. When people lie, they tend to cover their mouths. I learned that from Jack Webb when I was on Dragnet, 1970.'
jokes.setup: Artie coaches Larry on lying better to his staff
jokes.punchline: Artie cites Jack Webb from Dragnet 1970 as his source for body language expertise — treating a TV cop show credit as authoritative life wisdom
jokes.explanation: This is vintage Larry Sanders Show humor: Artie's old Hollywood credentialism played completely straight. The specificity of '1970' (not 'the '70s' but 1970) and naming Jack Webb elevates it from a generic old-timer joke to something with real texture. Artie treating a TV appearance as equivalent to professional training is a great character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It was during The mid-eighties, And I was carrying Some excess weight. And I had a persistent Skin rash, And it was hard for me To get dates.

jokes.text: Hank reveals to Artie and Larry that he's worried about the Hollywood Madam's black book going public: 'I mean, this whole Hollywood madam thing... if her black book ever goes public, I'm on every page of that thing.'
jokes.setup: Hank insists he doesn't need more rumors this week and launches into a seemingly unrelated concern
jokes.punchline: Hank casually drops that he's a regular — 'every page' — in the Hollywood Madam's black book
jokes.explanation: Rich character comedy. 'Every page' is an escalation that takes a scandalous admission and cranks it into absurdity. Hank's complete lack of shame about this is the joke — he's not confessing, he's just worried about logistics. Very Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Dick
dialogue.line: A late-night news magazine Wrap-up of the day's events, But with a hip, Mtv sensibility.

jokes.text: Artie asks: 'What are you listed under, Hank or Kingsley? Or hey, now?'
jokes.setup: Hank has revealed he's in the Hollywood Madam's black book on 'every page'
jokes.punchline: Artie mock-helpfully asks whether Hank used his name, his last name, or his catchphrase as his alias with prostitutes
jokes.explanation: The single funniest line in the episode. The punchline — 'Or hey, now?' — is perfect. It takes Hank's running catchphrase and weaponizes it as a punchline with devastating efficiency. The three-part structure (Hank, Kingsley, hey now) builds perfectly with the escalating absurdity. Only Artie could deliver this with exactly the right deadpan contempt. This is writing-room-level craft.

dialogue.speaker: Dick
dialogue.line: We can't make enough Of that shit.

jokes.text: Hank's wounded response: 'That's not very funny, you know. It was during the mid-eighties, and I was carrying some excess weight. And I had a persistent skin rash, and it was hard for me to get dates.'
jokes.setup: Artie has mocked Hank for being listed under 'hey now' in the Madam's book
jokes.punchline: Hank defends himself with a cascade of pathetic excuses — excess weight, a skin rash — that make it far more damning than if he'd just said nothing
jokes.explanation: Escalation gold. Hank begins with dignity ('That's not very funny, you know') and then destroys it himself with the most pathetic possible excuse list. 'Persistent skin rash' is a perfect detail — specific enough to be genuinely funny, pathetic enough to make the prostitute visits more depressing, not less. The line 'it was hard for me to get dates' after admitting he was a regular customer is the crown on the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I see what's wrong. You're drunk.

jokes.text: Artie reassures Larry the foreign buyer only wants to manage the news division, then suddenly breaks into a British accent to impersonate him: 'These talk shows, there are too damn many of them. I say let them have the territory. We can go out and, uh, blaze a new trail.'
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to calm Larry down about the new foreign network owner
jokes.punchline: Artie unexpectedly slips into a British accent impression of the buyer, voicing his dismissal of talk shows — which is exactly what Larry feared
jokes.explanation: A decent bit. Artie doing the impression while simultaneously trying to reassure Larry is funny because the impression undercuts his own reassurance. The 'blaze a new trail' phrase sets up the next joke well. Not the strongest in the episode but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Yes! Fuck that beer farm! We are out of here!

jokes.text: Larry asks what the 'new trail' is. Artie: 'A late-night news magazine wrap-up of the day's events, but with a hip, MTV sensibility.'
jokes.setup: Artie says the buyer wants to 'blaze a new trail' instead of keeping the talk show format
jokes.punchline: The 'new trail' is an utterly generic, buzzword-laden concept that sounds like something a beer-company executive would pitch
jokes.explanation: Good industry satire. 'Hip MTV sensibility' as the solution to every programming problem was already a cliché being mocked here. Sets up the meeting with Dick nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: I-- I live For this shit. It gets me all Hot and bothered.

jokes.text: Dick explains how he sold beer by rebranding it: 'One year it's beer. Then the next year we call it light beer. And then the next year it's cold-filtered or dry...' and concludes 'We can't make enough of that shit.'
jokes.setup: Dick is pitching Larry on why packaging/rebranding solves any problem
jokes.punchline: The beer analogy collapses into a gleeful vulgarity — 'we can't make enough of that shit' — that reveals Dick as someone who genuinely doesn't understand the difference between beer and television
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy and industry satire. The beer-label analogy for TV formatting is a precise skewering of corporate think applied to art. 'We can't make enough of that shit' lands because Dick is genuinely proud and completely unaware of how absurd he sounds. Classic clueless-executive archetype deployed with some specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You didn't see us. You saw nothing. You heard nothing. It's not what It looks like.

jokes.text: Larry's response to Dick's entire beer speech: 'I see what's wrong. You're drunk.'
jokes.setup: Dick has delivered an increasingly unhinged beer-branding monologue as a justification for changing Larry's show format
jokes.punchline: Larry cuts through all of it with the simplest, flattest diagnosis possible
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy. Six words that function as both a reasonable conclusion and a killer comeback. The deadpan confidence of the delivery is everything. This is exactly the kind of line Larry Sanders does better than anyone — the joke that sounds like a sincere observation. Economy score of 10 because not a syllable is wasted.

dialogue.line: the new Larry Sanders show, afternightline. Unfortunately, That's the actual title They wanna use.

jokes.text: Dick, stiffly: 'That is intended to be a joke, right?' Larry: 'Yeah, that's a joke. That's what I do for a living. Have you ever seen, uh, the show?'
jokes.setup: Larry has just called Dick drunk; Dick doesn't know how to process it
jokes.punchline: Larry confirms it's a joke then can't help but twist the knife: 'Have you ever seen, uh, the show?' — implying Dick doesn't even know what Larry does
jokes.explanation: Good follow-through on the previous joke. Larry's 'Have you ever seen, uh, the show?' is passive-aggressive gold — it's his way of asserting professional dignity while still being technically polite. The 'uh' is doing a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Great idea for a sitcom.

jokes.text: Beverly tells Larry his agent is waiting at his 'regular secret spot'
jokes.setup: Larry asks if his agent is there yet
jokes.punchline: Beverly refers to it as his 'regular secret spot' — meaning it's so regular it's not actually secret
jokes.explanation: A small, efficient joke about Larry's paranoia being so routine it's institutionalized. 'Regular secret spot' is an oxymoron that Beverly delivers completely straight. Understated and quick.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You ever see A scorsese film?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You know, Like goodfellas?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah.

jokes.text: Larry to his agent about Dick: 'I am not gonna be able to work for this fucking beer... nut.' Agent: 'Yes! Fuck that beer farm! We are out of here!'
jokes.setup: Larry is venting to his agent about the network buyer's beer-business mentality
jokes.punchline: Larry's mild 'beer nut' is instantly amplified by the agent's gonzo 'Fuck that beer farm!' — the agent's enthusiasm wildly outpacing Larry's complaint
jokes.explanation: 'Fuck that beer farm' is a genuinely great piece of absurdist escalation. Larry's 'beer nut' is already mild; the agent converting it to 'beer farm' with nuclear enthusiasm captures how Hollywood agents amplify everything for effect. The phrase 'beer farm' makes no sense and is funnier for it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What if we shoot In new jersey?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Even worse. They live there.

jokes.text: Agent: 'I live for this shit. It gets me all hot and bothered.'
jokes.setup: The agent has just declared 'We are out of here!' at Larry's crisis
jokes.punchline: Agent reveals his genuine enthusiasm for chaos and leverage — 'hot and bothered' — framing Larry's existential career crisis as personally thrilling
jokes.explanation: Good Hollywood agent characterization. The joke is that the agent's interests are perfectly misaligned with Larry's — Larry's crisis is the agent's fun. Functional but not as sharp as the 'beer farm' escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Hey, butt-bongo. Bravo!

jokes.text: A staffer walks in on Larry's secret meeting. Larry: 'You didn't see us. You saw nothing. You heard nothing. It's not what it looks like.'
jokes.setup: Larry and his agent are having a clandestine meeting in what is apparently a semi-public space
jokes.punchline: Larry's denial is so elaborate and specific — 'it's not what it looks like' — that it makes the mundane meeting sound far more scandalous
jokes.explanation: Larry's paranoia overdrive is always funny but this version of the joke is a bit generic. The escalating denials ('you saw nothing, you heard nothing') are standard fare. Functional character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Howard
dialogue.line: You're a big fan? Hey, take your top off.

jokes.text: Agent describes the ABC deal: 'the new Larry Sanders show, afterNightline.' He acknowledges: 'Unfortunately, that's the actual title they wanna use.'
jokes.setup: Agent is pitching the ABC alternative as a dream scenario for Larry
jokes.punchline: The proposed title is 'afterNightline' — so derivative and desperate it's embarrassing, and even the agent knows it
jokes.explanation: Solid industry satire — networks are so bad at branding they would literally name a show 'afterNightline.' The agent's embarrassed caveat ('unfortunately, that's the actual title') is a nice meta-acknowledgment. Clean joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The door that's marked 'can.'

jokes.text: Agent says ABC wants the show from New York. Larry: 'I'll give you another option: I go to Montana, live in a shack.' Agent: 'Great idea for a sitcom.'
jokes.setup: Larry rejects New York outright and offers Montana as a counteroffer
jokes.punchline: The agent responds to Larry's existential escape fantasy by immediately pitching it as an IP concept
jokes.explanation: Sharp Hollywood satire with excellent character integration. The agent can't process any statement that isn't a pitch opportunity — Montana shack becomes 'great idea for a sitcom.' It perfectly captures the industry's inability to let anything exist outside of commerce. The response is instantaneous, which is funnier than if he'd paused.

dialogue.speaker: Howard
dialogue.line: It's like she's Got something Shoved up her ass All the time. It's like she's On the perpetual rag.

jokes.text: Larry explains he can't go to New York, refuses to explain why, then the dialogue devolves: 'Well, I'm not asking you to explain. I just want to know why you can't go to New York.' / 'I can't explain.' / 'Well, don't explain. Just tell me.'
jokes.setup: Larry insists he can't go to New York but won't say why
jokes.punchline: The agent's distinction between 'explain' and 'tell me' collapses into circular logic that goes nowhere, perfectly capturing Hollywood non-communication
jokes.explanation: Good Pinter-esque dialogue exchange. 'Don't explain. Just tell me' is an absurdist non-distinction delivered as if it makes perfect sense. Captures the irrationality of how these two communicate. The joke is in the circularity.

dialogue.speaker: Jancis
dialogue.line: And I really think You should move The show to new york.

jokes.text: Larry's elaborate reason he can't go to New York: he was a young man, needed fast money, worked for 'some people' — 'You ever see a Scorsese film? Like Goodfellas?'
jokes.setup: Larry says what he's about to reveal could endanger both of them, with elaborate spy-thriller theatrics ('Turn around, Sid!')
jokes.punchline: The terrifying secret is that Larry apparently did mob work and can't return to New York because 'they live there' — delivered with complete gravity
jokes.explanation: Strong extended bit. The joke works on multiple levels: Larry's paranoid self-dramatization, the absurdity of a late-night host having mob entanglements, and the Scorsese reference as a sincere frame of reference. 'Turn around, Sid!' before the revelation is a great comic beat — the agent's driver is apparently a confidentiality risk. Very Larry Sanders in its commitment to its own internal logic.

dialogue.speaker: Jancis
dialogue.line: I think It'd be really good for us To have some time apart.

jokes.text: Agent: 'Oh, don't tell me this has something to do with a 50-pound bag of lime, for God's sake.'
jokes.setup: Larry is hinting darkly at mob work he did in New York
jokes.punchline: The agent immediately jumps to the most extreme mob-disposal imagery — suggesting this is not the first time he's had a conversation in this register with a client
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark joke. The specificity of '50-pound bag of lime' — the Hollywood shorthand for body disposal — delivered as a blasé 'Oh, don't tell me' suggests the agent is depressingly accustomed to this. The phrase 'for God's sake' makes it even funnier. High economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Howard
dialogue.line: well, I can reveal, for the first time, ladies and gentlemen... Larry Sanders will be taking his show to new york

jokes.text: Agent: 'What if we shoot in New Jersey?' Larry: 'Even worse. They live there.' Agent: 'Who? Who lives there?' Larry: 'I can't say.'
jokes.setup: The agent tries to solve the New York problem by suggesting New Jersey
jokes.punchline: New Jersey is rejected as 'even worse' because 'they live there' — an assertion Larry refuses to clarify
jokes.explanation: Good escalation on the mob bit. New Jersey being 'even worse' because the mob lives there is a funny geographic joke that also plays on real-life New Jersey mob stereotypes. Larry refusing to name them after already describing them in Scorsese terms is a nice sustained commitment to paranoid vagueness.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: He's taking us To new york.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: What if he's not Taking all of us?

jokes.text: Howard Stern appears and greets Larry: 'Hey, butt-bongo. Bravo!'
jokes.setup: Howard Stern arrives backstage as a guest
jokes.punchline: His greeting to Larry is 'butt-bongo' — a nonsense compliment/insult that only Howard Stern would use as an opening
jokes.explanation: The joke is almost entirely in the casting — Howard Stern playing himself saying something distinctly Howard Stern. 'Butt-bongo' is quintessentially his brand of absurdist vulgarity. Works because it's authentic, loses points on structure since it's just Stern being Stern.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: For making me Look like a liar In front of The entire staff. It was A real pleasure.

jokes.text: Larry coaches Stern not to mention 'that movie I'm doing, Fartman.' Stern: 'Everyone keeps asking me about it.' Larry: 'Yeah, I just don't want to talk about it. Ok, no on Fartman.'
jokes.setup: Standard pre-show briefing where host tells guest what not to discuss
jokes.punchline: The topic being avoided is 'Fartman' — a real Stern project that sounds too absurd to be real — and the word gets repeated multiple times with increasing comic weight
jokes.explanation: The joke is the word 'Fartman' repeated with complete professional gravity. Larry saying 'Ok, no on Fartman' and writing it down as if it's a normal pre-interview note is perfectly deadpan. The fact that Fartman was a real, notorious Stern project adds an extra layer. High character integration — this only works with Howard Stern.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You got a huge ass. It's a huge, huge ass. That's why we sent for That new lens from sony, So we could Cover that huge ass.

jokes.text: Larry to Sid after Stern leaves: 'It wouldn't hurt for you to laugh at me like that, Sid.' Sid gives a hollow, obligatory chuckle.
jokes.setup: Howard Stern just made everyone laugh by being outrageous; Larry notes the contrast with how people respond to him
jokes.punchline: Larry requests that his driver/companion laugh at him on command, revealing his desperate need for approval in the most naked possible way
jokes.explanation: A quietly devastating moment. Larry asking Sid to laugh at him on command, then Sid's compliant hollow chuckle, and Larry following up with 'Take your pants off' — a Stern impression that immediately falls flat — is a precise character study. It calls back to the intro ('because he desperately needs your approval') without saying so. High character integration: only Larry Sanders would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I have nightmares Of someone like you Coming through My window.

jokes.text: After requesting Sid laugh at him, Larry immediately tries a Stern impression: 'Take your pants off. Come on. Hey! Hey!'
jokes.setup: Larry has just asked Sid to laugh at him more the way people laugh at Stern
jokes.punchline: Larry tries to replicate Stern's success by doing the exact same bit Stern just did, demonstrating he cannot do it and doesn't understand why
jokes.explanation: The callback lands harder than the original. Larry mimicking Stern's 'take your top off' gag to his driver with zero of the charisma that makes it work is a perfect illustration of his insecurity. The joke is the gap between who Larry wishes he was and who he is.

dialogue.speaker: Chris Farley
dialogue.line: You're not going to amount To jack squat! You're gonna end up Eatin' a steady diet Of government cheese And livin' in a van Down by the river!

jokes.text: Howard Stern shows up at Larry's home unannounced. When Larry's partner answers, Stern says 'Trick or treat. Howard.' as a greeting.
jokes.setup: Doorbell rings at Larry's house; his partner answers expecting anyone but Howard Stern
jokes.punchline: 'Trick or treat. Howard.' — delivered as a genuine greeting, casual and absurd in equal measure
jokes.explanation: Efficient Stern character joke. 'Trick or treat' as a doorbell greeting — then the flat 'Howard' self-identification — captures his particular brand of performative weirdness. Economy is the strength here.

dialogue.speaker: Chris Farley
dialogue.line: I flew all the way in From new york for this. You know?

jokes.text: Larry's partner is horrified that Howard Stern is coming over: 'I don't want him around me. He's disgusting.' Larry: 'He's not like that in real life. That's just the way he is on the radio.'
jokes.setup: Larry's partner expresses revulsion at Stern's presence
jokes.punchline: Larry's defense — 'he's not like that in real life, that's just the way he is on the radio' — immediately collapses because Stern has already been exactly like that in real life in this very episode
jokes.explanation: Good structural irony. The audience has just watched Stern be exactly 'like that' in real life — 'butt-bongo,' 'take your top off.' Larry's earnest defense of Stern is contradicted by everything we've seen. The joke is entirely in the dramatic irony.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I knew it! It's new york!

jokes.text: After Stern leaves, he says of Larry's partner: 'she's got great tits, but... it's like she's got something shoved up her ass all the time. It's like she's on the perpetual rag.'
jokes.setup: Stern has just been the model houseguest; now alone with Larry, he reverts
jokes.punchline: The moment the partner leaves, Stern immediately delivers a deeply unflattering assessment — completing the comic whiplash between his public and private personas
jokes.explanation: The structural joke here is perfect — the misdirection of Stern being polite pays off here with the reveal of his actual assessment. The content of the joke is crass in Stern's signature way. The 'perpetual rag' line is vintage Stern. Loses points on 'earned vs cheap' because the content relies on lazy vulgarity, but the structure is solid.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: this is the final Larry Sanders show That you've watched tonight

jokes.text: Stern extracts the secret New York information through persistent 'casual' questioning: 'I would love to know if you're moving the show to New York.' Larry: 'I can't tell you.' After several rounds: Larry stays silent while Stern broadcasts it to millions.
jokes.setup: Larry has been carefully guarding information about possibly moving his show; Stern asks repeatedly with practiced innocence
jokes.punchline: Larry refuses to confirm but refuses to deny — and Stern, reading his non-response perfectly, has all the information he needs to broadcast
jokes.explanation: Good escalating cringe. Larry's paranoid information control collapses to someone doing a radio show from his living room. The dramatic irony of Larry being scrupulously vague while Stern broadcasts his non-denial live is sharp. Setup for the payoff of the staff hearing it on the radio.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: The name's darlene, You fucking idiot.

jokes.text: Dick calls Larry on the intercom: 'I hear this talk about you wanting to move to New York. It just makes me sad.' Then immediately: 'I do hope we can work things out, because you are legally bound to be with us for another 3 years, and I'd hate to see you spend the last 2 in court.'
jokes.setup: Dick opens with a conciliatory, emotionally manipulative tone about the New York rumors
jokes.punchline: The warmth evaporates instantly when Dick cites Larry's contractual obligations and threatens litigation in the same breath as 'I do hope we can work things out'
jokes.explanation: Excellent corporate double-speak joke. The pivot from 'it just makes me sad' to implicit legal threat is perfectly timed. 'I'd hate to see you spend the last 2 in court' — noting the 3-year contract and implying 1 year spent fighting — is almost elegant in its menace. The structure mimics how executives actually talk.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: The name's darlene, You fucking idiot.

jokes.text: Larry's partner tells him she thinks he should move the show to New York: 'I'm 100% behind it.' Larry: 'You think you'll be happy in New York?' Partner: '[beat]... I'm not gonna move to New York.'
jokes.setup: Larry's partner has been pushing Larry to move to New York for 'us'
jokes.punchline: When Larry turns the question back on her, she immediately clarifies she won't be going — she wants him to move to New York; she's staying in LA
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured revelation. The setup has her enthusiastically championing the move; the punchline is that she's actually trying to get rid of him. The beat between 'You think you'll be happy in New York?' and 'I'm not gonna move to New York' is doing enormous work. This is the episode's best relationship comedy — economical, unexpected, devastating.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You're a miserable fucker. A real miserable fucker.

jokes.text: Larry's partner, having revealed she wants space from Larry, then pivots: 'You know, I've been thinking about this all day long, and I think it'd be really good for us to have some time apart.' Then immediately backtracks: 'This is bad. I'm sorry. Just forget I brought it up.'
jokes.setup: The partner has just revealed she won't be moving to New York, meaning she was pushing Larry to move without her
jokes.punchline: She then explicitly says 'time apart' — breaking up with him mid-crisis — and immediately tries to unsay it when she sees the timing is terrible
jokes.explanation: Strong cringe beat. The relationship reveal compounds Larry's terrible day. 'This is bad. I'm sorry. Just forget I brought it up' while Larry processes both a career crisis and a breakup is good sustained discomfort comedy. The Larry Sanders Show excels at these layered, escalating bad days.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: * Da da, da-da, da da * And now, because He made a big mistake... Larry Sanders.

jokes.text: The intercom crackles — it's Howard Stern's live radio show broadcasting from Larry's living room, where Stern reveals Larry is moving his show to New York and going on after Nightline.
jokes.setup: Larry has just been hit with: the network threatening litigation, his partner revealing she wants to break up with him
jokes.punchline: Howard Stern — who was in his living room 20 minutes ago — has now broadcast everything Larry refused to confirm to the entire country
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Stern-at-Larry's-house sequence. The fact that Stern managed to extract and broadcast Larry's confidential career plans during what appeared to be a social visit is the perfect Stern joke — he's never off. The timing, landing during Larry's simultaneous personal and professional crisis, is well-orchestrated.

jokes.text: The staff hears the Stern broadcast. One staffer: 'He's taking us to New York.' Another: 'What if he's not taking all of us?' A third: 'That ass!'
jokes.setup: Staff overhears Howard Stern announcing Larry is moving the show to New York
jokes.punchline: The rapid escalation from 'he's taking us to New York' to 'what if he's NOT taking us' to 'that ass!' in seconds
jokes.explanation: Quick ensemble reaction beat. 'That ass!' is a funny explosion — the loyalty to Larry evaporates in under five seconds. Beverly's continued faith ('Larry wouldn't do that') vs. Phil's cynicism creates a good contrast. Functional group comedy.

jokes.text: The entire staff overhears Howard revealing the New York plan on the radio — Beverly insists 'that's pure speculation,' Hank says 'don't you think, if Larry's gonna take the show to New York, he'd tell me?'
jokes.setup: The staff hears Howard Stern's broadcast revealing Larry's secret plans
jokes.punchline: Beverly desperately defends Larry while Hank assumes he would be told — both are hilariously, obviously wrong. The audience knows Larry hasn't told either of them anything.
jokes.explanation: Good dramatic irony — the audience knows Larry tells nobody anything, so Hank's 'he'd tell me' and Beverly's 'pure speculation' land as sad/funny self-delusions. The reaction beat of the staff collectively processing the broadcast has comic value even if the individual lines aren't exceptional.

jokes.text: Hank corners Larry backstage: 'As you know, it's a higher cost of living in New York, and, um, I think that should be reflected in my, uh, paycheck.'
jokes.setup: Larry is rushing to do the show; Hank accosts him to negotiate
jokes.punchline: Hank is pre-negotiating a cost-of-living adjustment for a move that hasn't been decided and that he got from Howard Stern's radio show
jokes.explanation: Classic Hank opportunism. He hasn't even confirmed whether the move is real before demanding a raise for it. The 'as you know' opener — as if this is a formal negotiation — is perfect Hank self-importance. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: Agent explains why the ABC deal is only for one year: 'These guys never last. He'll be out of the job within a year. We renegotiate.' Larry: 'That makes no sense at all.'
jokes.setup: Larry questions why ABC would only offer a one-year deal
jokes.punchline: The agent's logic — sign a short deal because the executive offering it will be fired within the year anyway — is genuinely good Hollywood logic delivered as if it's completely sane
jokes.explanation: Sharp Hollywood insider comedy. The agent's logic is absurd but also uncomfortably accurate about how the industry works. Larry's 'That makes no sense at all' is right AND wrong simultaneously. Good industry satire.

jokes.text: Darlene asks if she'll still be able to go to New York if Larry and Hank go. Larry dismisses her with 'In a second, Darlene.' The moment he's gone, she mutters: 'The name's Darlene, you fucking idiot.'
jokes.setup: Darlene timidly asks if she'll have job security in the potential move
jokes.punchline: Larry doesn't even acknowledge her name — calls her 'Darlene' correctly but dismisses her completely — and Darlene's furious aside is directed at someone else entirely or reveals the full contempt she's been hiding
jokes.explanation: Good minor character eruption. 'The name's Darlene, you fucking idiot' — delivered presumably under her breath — is funny in its specificity and timing. The joke is that she's saying her name correctly in her own outburst, which implies she thinks Larry got it wrong (or doesn't know who she is at all). Delightful venting-from-below moment.

jokes.text: The agent tells Larry: 'You know what your problem is, Stevie? You talk to me like you think I believe you.'
jokes.setup: The agent (Stevie) is being dismissive of Larry's concerns about micromanaging
jokes.punchline: Larry calls out that the agent's confident salesmanship is performative — the explicit statement that he doesn't actually believe him
jokes.explanation: Sharp, quotable. 'You talk to me like you think I believe you' is a perfectly calibrated agent-client relationship joke. It captures the whole dynamic — the agent performing confidence, the client aware it's performance — in a single sentence. High economy and quotability.

jokes.text: Beverly confronts Larry before the show: 'I just wanted to say thanks. For making me look like a liar in front of the entire staff. It was a real pleasure.'
jokes.setup: Beverly has been covering for Larry all day, telling the staff he knows nothing
jokes.punchline: Stern's radio broadcast exposed everything Beverly denied, and she delivers her thanks with maximum biting sarcasm
jokes.explanation: Good character moment. Beverly's sarcasm is earned — she's been actively lying for Larry and got burned. 'It was a real pleasure' is the right button. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Artie confronts Larry in the wings during the warm-up: 'You got a huge ass. It's a huge, huge ass. That's why we sent for that new lens from Sony, so we could cover that huge ass.'
jokes.setup: Larry snaps at Artie about not being kept informed; Artie fires back
jokes.punchline: Artie, perfectly timed to be whispered during live warm-up, attacks Larry's ass and reveals the Sony lens cover story — a brutal producer's confession disguised as practical logistics
jokes.explanation: Excellent Artie moment. The attack on Larry's ass is crude but the reveal that they got a special wide-angle Sony lens to accommodate it is the brilliant escalation — it turns a personal insult into a logistical detail. 'Huge, huge ass' with the repetition is funnier than one 'huge.' Artie delivering this in the wings during live warm-up makes it better.

jokes.text: Larry introduces Chris Farley (SNL) by listing his credits: 'I love everything you do on Saturday Night Live. I love the—' then pivots: 'I have nightmares of someone like you coming through my window.'
jokes.setup: Larry is doing the standard host intro, listing what he loves about the guest
jokes.punchline: Mid-compliment, Larry's genuine terror of Farley's physicality escapes: 'I have nightmares of someone like you coming through my window'
jokes.explanation: Sharp misdirection with strong character integration. The left turn from 'I love everything you do' to 'I have nightmares of someone like you coming through my window' is perfectly Larryesque — complimentary on the surface, terrified underneath. The joke works on Farley's specific physicality without being mean-spirited.

jokes.text: Chris Farley's motivational speaker character description/performance: '...you're gonna end up eating a steady diet of government cheese and living in a van down by the river!'
jokes.setup: Farley explains the motivational speaker character is based on his father
jokes.punchline: The full delivery of the van-down-by-the-river speech, building from 'take the world by the tail' to the crushing 'government cheese' conclusion
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's crown jewel and one of the most iconic bits in the history of SNL-adjacent television comedy. 'Living in a van down by the river' became a permanent part of the American comedy lexicon. The structure is perfect: the inspirational build ('take the world by the tail') demolished by the specificity and pathos of 'government cheese' and the van. Farley's physical commitment is legendary. By the calibration standard, this is absolutely comparable to the 9.5/10 anchor — it became a cultural touchstone. The episode essentially exists partly to get to this moment.

jokes.text: Farley, after Larry starts wrapping: 'I thought maybe it was gonna be longer. I thought— I've only been out here a couple minutes. Is that how it—Er, uh...' Larry: 'It is a little short.'
jokes.setup: Larry has begun cutting off Farley's segment
jokes.punchline: Farley's confused, wounded reaction — the Farley puppy-dog disappointment that was his trademark — and Larry's honest 'It is a little short' agreement
jokes.explanation: Good awkward beat. Farley's puppyish 'I thought it was gonna be longer' is perfect — the over-eager performer who wanted more time. Larry admitting 'It is a little short' while still cutting him is perfectly Larry: honest, selfish, oblivious.

jokes.text: Farley protests: 'I flew all the way in from New York for this.' Larry: 'You flew in from New York? How long is that flight?' Then staff immediately: 'I knew it! It's New York!'
jokes.setup: Farley is complaining about flying from New York for a short segment
jokes.punchline: Larry's genuine interest in the flight time is immediately weaponized by staff as confirmation of the show's move to New York
jokes.explanation: Nice callback to the running New York anxiety. The absurdity of 'how long is that flight?' being construed as a New York admission is perfectly tuned to the staff's paranoia level. The non-sequitur jump works because we've earned it through the whole episode's anxiety.

jokes.text: Larry announces on air that 'this is the final Larry Sanders Show' and he's retiring to Montana 'to live the rest of my life as just an everyday guy.'
jokes.setup: The episode has been about Larry's future — network sale, possible New York move, relationship breakdown
jokes.punchline: Larry, in a moment of crisis-induced impulsiveness, announces his retirement on live TV — to thunderous audience applause — choosing Montana
jokes.explanation: The Montana callback pays off beautifully. What started as a throwaway joke ('great idea for a sitcom') becomes Larry's actual public declaration. It's a character-rich joke: Larry is so overwhelmed he goes nuclear, and the audience's thunderous approval — 'Approval! He desperately needs it' — makes it bittersweet. Excellent structural callback.

jokes.text: Larry announces on air that this is the 'final Larry Sanders Show' — a fake retirement speech with a full staff thank-you — then reveals: 'If anyone needs me, I'll be in Montana.'
jokes.setup: Larry, still mid-show and facing pressure from all directions, suddenly announces he's retiring
jokes.punchline: The faux-retirement speech — delivered with full gravitas, acknowledging the staff — ends with the Montana punchline, revealing this is both theater and Larry's genuine fantasy of escape
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the Montana thread. Larry's on-air retirement speech is a beautiful piece of character comedy: he's using the live show as therapy, performing his fantasy of escape for a studio audience. The callback to Montana gives it emotional and comedic weight. Also meta — this is a show about a show, and Larry is doing something completely absurd on live TV while his staff watches in confusion.

jokes.text: During his tearful on-air goodbye, Larry spots Farley backstage and whispers: 'Hey, Chris. Listen, I have some sketch ideas. Could you take 'em down to SNL?'
jokes.setup: Larry is giving an emotional farewell speech live on air
jokes.punchline: Mid-speech, he breaks to hustle Farley for an SNL connection — pure Hollywood opportunism that can't even be suppressed during his own retirement announcement
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character moment. Larry's inability to suppress his Hollywood instincts even during his own live TV retirement is perfectly observed. He's announcing his return to humanity while simultaneously networking. The line is quick, quiet, conspiratorial — making it funnier than if it were a big moment. Very quotable.

jokes.text: In the middle of his retirement tribute, Larry 'acknowledges' Darlene with 'the rest of the office staff' — not by name. Darlene, on camera: 'The name's Darlene, you fucking idiot.'
jokes.setup: Larry is going through his sentimental farewell, naming key people
jokes.punchline: When he gets to the support staff he lumps Darlene into 'and the rest of the office staff' — she gets her name wrong (or ignored) again, and this time says her piece on camera
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Darlene name joke is enormously satisfying. The callback structure is clean: she muttered it earlier, now she says it to his face (or to camera) during his live retirement broadcast. 'The name's Darlene, you fucking idiot' is one of the most quotable lines of the episode. The escalation from quiet fury to public declaration is earned.

jokes.text: Artie, after the show, to Larry: 'You're a miserable fucker. A real miserable fucker.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just retired on live television in a moment of panic and self-pity
jokes.punchline: Artie's entire assessment of the situation — and possibly Larry's whole life — delivered twice, with the second iteration adding nothing but emphasis and gravity
jokes.explanation: Right up there with the 'hey now' line as the episode's best. The repetition — 'A real miserable fucker' — is doing everything. It's not emphasis, it's a kind of loving assessment, a diagnosis. Only Artie can call Larry a miserable fucker with the warmth of a mentor. The pause between the two sentences is everything. Maximum character integration: this is Rip Torn's line and no one else could deliver it. Exceptional economy. The whole episode is summarized in eight words.

jokes.text: Scene cut to Montana fishing. Larry is actually in Montana. He falls into the river ('Shit.'). A fisherman hushes him: 'You're scaring the fish.'
jokes.setup: Larry has announced he's going to Montana to live as 'just an everyday guy'
jokes.punchline: He's in Montana, falling into a river, and his attempt to apologize for splashing scares the fish — he can't even exist in nature without causing problems
jokes.explanation: The Montana sequence is a beautifully executed structural callback. Larry actually went to Montana — the extreme impulse followed through — and is immediately terrible at it. Falling into the river, being shushed by a stranger about scaring fish, is perfectly calibrated to his character. He can't win anywhere.

jokes.text: The fisherman asks Larry: 'You watch TV much?' Larry doesn't answer. Then: 'Stay up late?'
jokes.setup: Larry and a random fisherman are fishing together in Montana
jokes.punchline: The fisherman asks two questions that are clearly about to reveal he knows who Larry is — and Larry's silent non-response to each creates a sustained cringe beat
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed. 'You watch TV much?' followed by 'Stay up late?' is the perfect two-step approach — the fisherman is clearly recognizing Larry, and the pause between each question is where the joke lives. Larry's silence is the funniest response possible. Superb economy: six words in two questions tell us everything.

jokes.text: Larry, unprompted, starts humming his own theme song to the fisherman: 'Da da, da-da, da da... Mmm-hmm, mm-mm, mm-hmm.'
jokes.setup: The fisherman has just asked oblique questions suggesting he might recognize Larry
jokes.punchline: Larry hums his own show's theme music — identifying himself by his theme song rather than his name — an act of pure, helpless self-promotion in the middle of nature
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's emotional and comedic apex, tied with Artie's 'miserable fucker.' Larry has fled to Montana to escape show business and within minutes he is humming his own theme song to a stranger in a river. It's the perfect crystallization of the entire show: he cannot exist without the approval, without the identity, without the show. It requires no dialogue — just the theme music hummed by the man who fled it. 10 on character integration because this is literally the thesis of Larry Sanders made physical. Exceptional structure, originality, and character specificity.

jokes.text: The fisherman does a Larry Sanders-style announcer intro over the river: 'And now, because he made a big mistake... Larry Sanders.' Frogs croak. Larry: 'Fucking frogs.'
jokes.setup: The fisherman has recognized Larry from the theme-song hum; he does a mock announcer intro
jokes.punchline: He mirrors Hank's opening intro — but where Hank said 'because he desperately needs your approval,' the fisherman says 'because he made a big mistake' — then the theme plays and frogs croak as the 'audience.' Larry: 'Fucking frogs.'
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke, and one of the best closing gags in the show's run. It's a perfect structural callback to the opening announcer intro — 'because he desperately needs your approval' becomes 'because he made a big mistake.' The variation is devastating: not just funny but a complete thematic statement about the episode. The frogs croaking as the 'audience applause' and Larry's flat 'Fucking frogs' is the cherry. This is writing at the highest level: a callback that recontextualizes the opening, a visual gag (frogs as audience), character comedy, and a thematic coda all at once. Comparable to the 9.5/10 anchor.

tmdb_overview: Larry seriously considers either quitting the biz or moving his show to New York after the network's new owner begins to meddle with the format.
